PART1

Interview Studio

Lead the interview in clear, global English: sound simple, sound kind, and practise every phrase out loud.

Your goals today

By the end you can…

  • Explain the purpose of a continuity interview in plain, global English.
  • Ask the right question at each section of the process form.
  • Rescue a conversation when the listener is lost.
  • Match real situations to the four impact types — and suggest a solution.

Warm-up: think first

  1. Which part of your interviews do people find most difficult to understand?
  2. What words do you replace when someone says “sorry, I don’t understand”?
  3. How would you explain “critical” to a colleague who speaks English as a third language?

Think about your answers for one minute. You will test them in the Studio.

Why simple English wins

Your audience is global: colleagues in Greece, France, Spain and beyond. For most of them English is a second or third language. In this interview, clarity is more important than elegance.

In daily operations, everything is essential. In a crisis, only a fraction is vital.

🎧 Model opening — listen, then shadow it

This is a 60-second opening in global English. Listen once, then speak along with the voice (try “Slow”).

Six golden rules for a global audience

Press 🔊 to hear each “Say” sentence. Repeat it out loud — your mouth must know it before the interview.

1

One idea per sentence.

AvoidPlease think about the worst case because if the process has a peak or a deadline and it is blocked in that period the problem is bigger so we should not think about a normal day.
SayPlease think about the worst case. For example, a deadline. If the process stops then, the problem is bigger.
2

Choose the common word.

AvoidThe application is indisposable. I have necessity to understand.
SayThe application is unavailable. I need to understand.
3

Skip idioms and slang.

AvoidDon’t worry, it’s a piece of cake.
SayDon’t worry. It is easy, and I will help you.
4

Signpost every step.

Avoid(silence) …and now the impact.
SayFirst, we describe the process. Next, we look at systems. Finally, we talk about impact.
5

Check understanding often.

AvoidYou understand, right?
SayJust to check — does that make sense? Please tell me in your own words.
6

Slow down. Pause. Give an example.

AvoidCritical means the activity is indispensable for continuity.
SayCritical means: if it stops, the company has a serious problem. For example, if your only supplier disappears.

The interview map

The process form has twelve sections. Here is what to say at each stage — in simple English, ready to practise.

1 · Opening — Before the form
Goal: Welcome the person, explain the purpose and set the pace.
Thank you for joining. My name is Annadora, and I work in Business Continuity.
Today we will complete a short form about your process. It will take about an hour.
Please note that this meeting is recorded, so we have a backup of the information.“Backup” = a copy, so nothing is lost.
We are not judging your work. We want to understand what happens if your process stops.
If I speak too fast or use a difficult word, please stop me.
2 · Sites & description — Form sections 1–2
Goal: Where do people work, and what does the process do?
Which office do you work from?
If that office is not available, can your team work from home?Smart working = working from home.
In two or three sentences, what does your process do?
3 · Focal points & peaks — Form sections 3–4
Goal: Who to call first, and when is the busiest time?
Who is the first person we call in an emergency?Focal point = first contact.
And who is the backup for this person?
Are there busy periods — for example, the end of the month or the end of the year?
When exactly does the peak start and end?
4 · Inputs & outputs — Form sections 5–6
Goal: Who sends work in, and who receives results?
Which teams send you information or data?
Which teams receive your results?
What do they need from you, and how often?
5 · Applications — Form section 7
Goal: Which systems are needed — and can the team work without them?
Which applications do you use every day?
If this application is unavailable, can you still do your work?
Do you have a workaround — another way to do the same task?
How quickly do you need the system back?RTO = recovery time.
How much data can you afford to lose?RPO = how far back the data must go.
6 · People — Form section 8
Goal: Is the process dependent on specific individuals?
Does anyone else know how to do this work?
Does your backup have all the skills needed?
How long would it take to train a replacement?
7 · Third parties — Form section 9
Goal: Which vendors support the process, and can they be replaced?
Which external companies support this process?
Is this vendor exclusive? Can you replace them with another company?
If the vendor is unavailable, how long can you wait?MAO/MTPD = the longest outage that is acceptable.
8 · Assets & shared folders — Form sections 10–11
Goal: Equipment and the places where important files live.
Which equipment do you need — for example, laptop, phone or tablet?
Where do you save your files — for example, a SharePoint or network folder?
If you cannot open that folder, can you still work?
9 · Impact — Form section 12
Goal: The heart of the interview: when does a stop become serious?
Imagine the worst moment of the year. Your process stops for eight hours. What happens?
What if it stops for one day? For two days?
Think about four types of impact: operative loss, competitive loss, compliance impact, and reputational impact.
At what point does the damage become serious?
10 · Closing — After the form
Goal: Summarise, check, and thank.
Let me summarise what I understood. Please correct me if something is wrong.
Is there anything I missed?
Thank you for your time. I will send you the notes by email.

Say it simply: makeovers

First drafts are normal. Tap a card to flip it, listen to both versions, and notice what changed: shorter sentences, common words, one question at a time.

Typical first draft

Do you know the business continuity?

Tap to flip ⟳
Global-ready version

Are you familiar with business continuity? In short: it is a plan for keeping the company working in a crisis.

Typical first draft

In this section I search the unit that have contact with this process in input and output.

Tap to flip ⟳
Global-ready version

In this section, we look at two things: which teams send you information, and which teams receive your results.

Typical first draft

The system is critical if it is indisposable and you don’t have a workaround.

Tap to flip ⟳
Global-ready version

A system is critical when it is unavailable and you have no other way to work.

Typical first draft

How many times the process can be blocked to don’t have a problem for the company?

Tap to flip ⟳
Global-ready version

How long can the process stop before the company has a serious problem?

Typical first draft

For default everyone says their process is important.

Tap to flip ⟳
Global-ready version

I know every process feels important to its owner. Today we are asking a different question.

Typical first draft

We consider the worst case. If there is a peak and it blocks, it is the most important problem.

Tap to flip ⟳
Global-ready version

Please think about the worst moment, for example a deadline. If the process stops then, the problem is bigger.

Phrase vault

ExpressionMeaning (plain English)Example
criticalessential; without it the company has a serious problem“Is this application critical for your process?”
workaroundanother way to do the task when the normal way is not available“If the system is down, do you have a workaround?”
backupa person or system that can replace the main one“Who is your backup if you are on holiday?”
focal pointthe first person to call in an emergency“Who is the focal point for this process?”
peakthe busiest period“The peak is at the end of the month.”
deadlinethe last moment to finish something“The report has a deadline on Friday.”
downtime / outagea period when a system or service does not work“A two-day outage would be a serious problem.”
vendor / third partyan external company that supplies a service“Which vendors support this process?”
exclusivethe only one; there is no alternative in the market“Is this vendor exclusive?”
worst casethe most difficult realistic situation“Think about the worst case, for example a deadline.”
impactthe effect on the company if something goes wrong“What is the impact if the process stops for a day?”
unavailablecannot be used or reached“The system is unavailable.”
recoveryreturning to normal after a problem“How fast must the recovery be?”
finemoney that an authority makes a company pay“The company may receive a fine.”
mandatoryrequired by law or by a rule“Business continuity is mandatory under EU rules.”

🛟 Rescue phrases — when the listener is lost

Let me say that in a simpler way.Does that make sense?Would an example help?Take your time.Could you say it in your own words?Sorry, I didn’t catch that. Could you repeat it?Let me repeat the key point.Just a moment — let me write that down.Could you give me a concrete example?Please stop me if a word is unclear.

The risk lens: four pillars, one clock

Every question in the interview serves one idea: how long can this process stop before the damage is serious? We measure the damage in four ways.

Operative loss

Money and work stop.

Competitive loss

Clients leave.

Compliance impact

A fine from an authority.

Reputational impact

Public trust is damaged.

🌍 Speaking to a global audience

Many colleagues understand written English better than spoken English. Share your screen, type key words in the chat, and give people time to read before you move on. Avoid sarcasm and jokes that depend on culture.

📜 Why it is mandatory

European rules such as DORA and NIS 2 push companies to prove they can keep working in a crisis. Explain this in one sentence: “It is a rule, so it has to be followed.”

PART2

Risk Detective

Fix the patterns that change meaning — do / does, -s, passive, if-clauses — and analyse two risk cases.

Your mission

By the end you can…

  • Use do / does / don’t / doesn’t and the third-person -s accurately — in statements and in questions.
  • Use passive + modals, if-clauses, and time expressions accurately.
  • Replace Italian look-alikes with the right English word.
  • Describe risk with 19 high-value expressions.
  • Read a story, find the dependencies, and complete a process form.

Warm-up: spot the pattern

  1. Say aloud: “The process can blocked for many times.” What feels wrong?
  2. How do you say “indisponibile” in English?
  3. Complete: “If the vendor stops, the process …”

Think first. Then check your instincts in the Pattern clinic.

Pattern clinic

Ten patterns that make an interview sound precise. No rules to memorise — just a formula, a picture, and sentences to say aloud.

Coach tip: “Draft” sentences are not wrong ideas — they are ideas in transit. Press 🔊 on the “Better” line and copy the music of the sentence.
1

Say what happens to the process

DraftThe process can blocked for eight hours.
BetterThe process can be blocked for eight hours.
thing+can / may / will+be+past participle
A cyber attack
→ blocks →
the process
ACTIVE — the doer comes first
The process
→ can be blocked →
(by a cyber attack)
PASSIVE — the affected thing comes first; the doer is optional
SayThe data can be lost.
SayThe vendor may be replaced.
SayThe plan will be activated.
SayThe report was delayed.
2

How long? vs. How often?

DraftThe process can be blocked for many times.
BetterThe process can be blocked for a long time / for several hours.
How long?for+ a period|How often?(many) times · every month
⏱ HOW LONG?
for eight hours
for a long time
up to 24 hours
more than two days
🔁 HOW OFTEN?
many times a year
every month
twice a week
“Times” counts repetitions. A period of time needs for.
SayHow long can the process stop?
SayIt stopped for two days.
SayIt has happened three times this year.
SayThe impact becomes serious after eight hours.
3

Negatives: don’t · doesn’t · can’t

DraftThis process don’t can be blocked for long time.
BetterThis process can’t be blocked for a long time. / It doesn’t have a workaround.
I · you · we · theydon’t|he · she · it · the processdoesn’t+ verb|anyonecan’t+ verb
We
They
The teams
→
don’t have
The process
The vendor
She
→
doesn’t have
Everyone
→
can’t work  (never “don’t can”)
SayThe company doesn’t have a plan.
SayThe teams don’t have a backup.
SayThe vendor can’t restore the service today.
SayThis process doesn’t depend on one person.
4

Questions: Do you…? Does the process…?

DraftDoes the people have a backup? Your backup have the skills? Where work the people?
BetterDo the people have a backup? Does your backup have the skills? Where do the people work?
(Question word)Do+ I · you · we · they · plural+ base verb|(Question word)Does+ he · she · it · the process+ base verb
The vendor provides a backup.
→
Does the vendor provide a backup?
The -s moves to does. The main verb goes back to its base form — never “does … provides”.
Which systems do you use?
Where does the team work?
When does the peak start?
SayDo you have a backup?
SayDoes the process have a workaround?
SayDoes your backup have all the skills?
SayWhich systems do you use every day?
SayWhen does the peak start?
SayWhere does the team work?
5

Past: was · were · did · didn’t

DraftThe workers was died in the factory. The system don’t work yesterday. Did the vendor restored it?
BetterTwo workers died in the factory. The system didn’t work yesterday. Did the vendor restore it?
I · he · she · it · processwas|you · we · they · pluralwere|did / didn’t+ base verb(no -ed)
The system was down.
The servers were down.
The vendor restored it.
→
Did the vendor restore it?
→
It didn’t restore it.
After did / didn’t the verb is in its base form: the “past” is already inside did.
SayThe system was unavailable yesterday.
SayThe servers were down for two hours.
SayWe didn’t receive the data.
SayDid the vendor restore the service?
6

There is / There are · no · unable to

DraftPeople don’t have the possibility to activate the contract. There are a contact with clients.
BetterCustomers are unable to activate the contract. There is contact with clients.
There is+ singular / uncountable|There are+ plural|There is no+ noun|are unable to / cannot+ verb
There is no workaround.
There is one vendor.
There are two backups.
There are many risks.
Say “there is no way / no workaround” instead of “don’t have the possibility”.
SayThere is no workaround.
SayThere are two trained backups.
SayCustomers are unable to sign the contract.
SayThere is only one vendor in the market.
7

Need · have to · must

DraftI have necessity to understand the process.
BetterI need to understand the process.
need to+ verb|It is necessary to+ verb|must / have to+ verb
want to
→
should
→
need to
→
have to
→
must = mandatory
Stronger → rules and laws use “must” and “mandatory”.
SayWe need to know who the backup is.
SayYou have to send the report on Friday.
SayBusiness continuity is mandatory.
SayWe must test the plan every year.
8

If + present → will

DraftIf the company don’t have this activity, the company don’t know the plan.
BetterIf the company doesn’t have this activity, it won’t know when to activate the plan.
If+ present simple,will+ verb|General truth: If+ present, present
IF the vendor stops
→
THEN the delay will grow
IF there is a workaround
→
the system is not critical
Never “If … will”: after “if”, use the present.
SayIf the vendor stops, the process will stop.
SayIf there is a workaround, the system is not critical.
SayIf the office is closed, we can work from home.
SayIf the report is late, the company may receive a fine.
9

who · that · -s

DraftThe people that work in this process … The unit that this process send the data.
BetterThe people who work in this process … The unit that this process sends the data to …
peoplewho+ verb|things / teamsthat+ verb|he / she / it / process+ verb-s
👤 the person who works
⚙ the system that stops
the process sends-s
Third person singular always takes -s: it sends, she works, the vendor provides.
SayThe person who knows the process is Maria.
SayThe vendor that supports us is exclusive.
SayThe process sends data to the finance team.
SayThe teams that receive our results need them daily.

Italian look-alikes

Some Italian words look almost English — and quietly change the meaning. These eleven appear again and again in continuity work.

ITALIAN

indisponibile

→ unavailable
not “indisposable”

“The system is unavailable.”

ITALIAN

compilare

→ fill in / complete
not “compile”

“Please fill in the form.”

ITALIAN

sede

→ site / office / headquarters
not “seat”

“Which site do you work from?”

ITALIAN

obbligatorio

→ mandatory / compulsory
“obligatory” is rare

“Business continuity is mandatory.”

ITALIAN

fabbrica

→ factory
“fabric” = cloth

“A serious accident at the factory.”

ITALIAN

carburante

→ fuel
not “carburant”

“The fuel price cap.”

ITALIAN

centrale elettrica

→ power plant
not “electrical central”

ITALIAN

danno

→ damage
not “danno impact”

ITALIAN

→ possible

“A possible delay.”

ITALIAN

→ currently

“We are currently testing it.”

ITALIAN

→ significant loss
“important” is weaker

“A significant loss of revenue.”

Vocabulary toolkit

ExpressionMeaningExample
single point of failureone part that, if it fails, stops everything“The vendor is a single point of failure.”
downtimetime when a system is not working“Every hour of downtime costs money.”
outagea sudden stop of a service“The outage lasted two days.”
disruptiona problem that interrupts normal work“A pandemic can cause serious disruption.”
restoreto bring a service back“The vendor will restore the service tomorrow.”
workaroundanother way to do the task when the normal way fails“We use a spreadsheet as a workaround.”
fallbacka second plan for when the first one fails“We need a fallback plan for the portal.”
redundancyextra capacity that can replace a failed part“The servers have redundancy.”
mitigateto make a risk smaller“A second vendor can mitigate the risk.”
escalateto report a problem to a higher level“Please escalate the incident to the director.”
dependencysomething a process needs in order to work“The process has a strong dependency on one vendor.”
contingency plana plan for an emergency“The contingency plan includes a manual procedure.”
backlogwork that is waiting to be done“After the outage we had a large backlog.”
exposurehow much a company can lose if a risk happens“Our exposure to this vendor is high.”
safeguardsomething that protects“Offline backups are a safeguard.”
breacha failure to follow a rule, or a security failure“A data breach must be reported.”
penaltymoney you pay for breaking a rule or missing a deadline“Late reports can bring a penalty.”
MAO / MTPDthe longest outage or disruption the company can tolerate“The MAO of this process is 24 hours.”
RTO / RPOhow fast a system must return / how much recent data you can lose“The RTO is four hours.”

Case files: risk detective

Two short stories. Read (and listen to) each one, hover over the highlighted words, then complete the process form like a risk analyst: find the dependencies, then decide when the damage becomes serious.

Case A · Friday at the Athens desk

It is the last working day of the month in the Athens office. If the office is closed, the team can work from home. Maria’s team must prepare the monthly invoices and send a report to the energy authority before 9 a.m. tomorrow. Email and video calls work normally, but everything else depends on one billing platform. At 10 a.m. the platform becomes unavailable because the provider has suffered a cyber attack. The provider is the only company that can run this platform. The team has no manual workaround: the invoices cannot be created on paper or in a spreadsheet. Maria is the only person who knows how to run the final upload. Her backup, Yiannis, joined last month and has not been trained yet. Maria also saves all customer files in one shared network folder, which is hosted on the same platform. If the platform stays down for more than one day, the report will be late, customers will not receive their bills, and the company may receive a fine.

0

Case B · The only supplier

In the Lyon office, the sales team sells new energy offers online. If the office is closed, the team can work from home. Email and phones work normally, and each person has a laptop and a phone. The website receives customer data from only one vendor, the sole provider of this service in the region. In winter, when the news announces lower fuel prices, thousands of customers visit the website at the same time. This year, during the busiest week, the vendor’s data centre was flooded. The vendor says it needs three days to restore the service. There is no other way to receive customer data. Meanwhile, a competitor has launched a cheaper offer, and customers are asking for help on social media. The process owner, Camille, has two trained backups, so people are not the problem.

0

Part 1 · Interview Studio

Exercise 1 · Memory game
  • downtime ↔ hourglass
  • financial loss ↔ scales and ledger
  • we lose clients to a competitor ↔ sinking ship and lifeboat
  • regulatory fine ↔ gavel and certificate
  • reputational damage ↔ cracked shield
  • there is no workaround ↔ rope bridge over a cliff
  • vulnerability ↔ broken machinery
  • focal point ↔ desk with notes
Exercise 2 · Click-to-match
  • workaround — another way to do the task when the system is down
  • backup — a person or system that can replace the main one
  • peak — the busiest period
  • outage — a period when a service does not work
  • vendor — an external company that supplies a service
  • exclusive — the only one; nobody can replace it
  • deadline — the last moment to finish something
  • critical — essential; without it the company has a serious problem
Exercise 3 · Fill in the blank
  1. Which office do you work from?
  2. If the system is unavailable, do you have a workaround ?
  3. Who is your backup if you are on holiday?
  4. When does the peak start — the busiest period?
  5. Is this vendor exclusive? Can we replace them?
  6. Please think about the worst case, for example a deadline.
  7. How long can the process stop before there is a serious problem?
  8. Let me make sure I understood correctly.
Exercise 4 · True / False
  1. False — Short sentences with one idea are easier to follow for people who speak English as a second language.
  2. True — An example turns an abstract word into a picture.
  3. False — Idioms often do not translate. Say: “It is easy.”
  4. True — It is a gentle way to find out if the listener is lost.
  5. False — We evaluate the impact of absence, not the quality of daily work.
  6. False — We calibrate on the worst case: a deadline or a peak.
  7. True — Seeing and hearing the word together doubles the support.
  8. False — One question at a time. Wait for the answer.
Exercise 5 · Clearest question
  1. “How long can the process stop before the company has a serious problem?” — Short, common words, correct grammar. “How long” asks about duration.
  2. “Do you have a backup? Can this person do all your tasks?” — Two short, direct questions. “Out of the picture” is an idiom and the second option has a grammar problem.
  3. “If the application is unavailable, can you still do your work in another way?” — “Unavailable” is the standard word, and the question order is natural.
  4. “Is this vendor exclusive? Can you replace it with another company?” — “Exclusive” is a form term, and the second question explains it in plain words.
  5. “When are your busiest periods? For example, the end of the month?” — Plain vocabulary plus an example. The first option has a word-order problem.
  6. “Imagine your process stops for eight hours at your busiest moment. What happens?” — It paints a concrete scene (worst case) and ends with a simple question.
Exercise 6 · Everyday interview moments
  1. “Sorry, I didn’t catch that. Could you repeat it, please?”
  2. “Just a moment, please — let me write that down.”
  3. “I understand — every process matters. Let’s think about the worst case: what happens after eight hours?”
  4. “Just to check — does that make sense?”
  5. “Could you give me a concrete example?”
  6. “We have about five minutes left, so let me ask my last questions.”
  7. “Let me summarise what I understood. Please correct me if something is wrong.”
Exercise 7 · Dialogue

Annadora: Hello Elena, thank you for joining. Can you hear me well?
Elena: Yes, I can. Sorry, my English is a little slow.
Annadora: No problem at all. I will speak slowly. First, who is the focal point for this process — the person we call first in an emergency?
Elena: That is me, and my backup is Carlos.
Annadora: Thank you. Now, think about the busiest time of the year. When is the peak?
Elena: At the end of the month, because of the invoice deadline.
Annadora: Good. Let’s imagine the worst case: the billing system is unavailable for one day. Can you work in another way?
Elena: No, we have no workaround.
Annadora: I see. And who supports the system? Is it an external vendor?
Elena: Yes, and it is exclusive. Only one company can do this.
Annadora: Thank you, that is very clear. This looks like a critical process. Let me summarise what I understood.

Exercise 8 · Written production

Model answer: Every process is important in daily work, but not every process is critical. A process is critical when the company has a serious problem very quickly if it stops. For example, if your office is closed, you can work from home, so the problem is small. However, if your only supplier disappears, there is no other way to work, and the delay can last many days. In other words, we are not asking how important your work is. We are asking what happens when it stops.

Exercise 9 · Case files
  1. The Frozen Portal — Competitive loss. Solution: Open a phone and email channel for signing contracts, and test it every year.
  2. The Missed Report — Compliance impact. Solution: Train the backup and write a step-by-step procedure.
  3. The Locked Drive — Operative loss. Solution: Keep regular offline backups in a separate, secure place.
  4. The Silent Hotline — Reputational impact. Solution: Sign with a second vendor and prepare an internal emergency team.
  5. The Missing Data — Operative loss. Solution: Prepare an exit plan: a backup supplier or an approved temporary estimate method.
  6. The Silent Alarm — Reputational impact. Solution: Create a manual alert procedure — radios, a phone tree, regular drills.
Exercise 10 · Dictation
  1. Let me make sure I understood correctly.
  2. If your process stops, how quickly does the company face a serious problem?
  3. Is this vendor exclusive, or can you replace it with another company?
  4. Please think about the worst case, for example a deadline.
  5. This meeting is recorded, so we have a backup of the information.
Interview simulator · best replies
  1. No problem, Nikos. I will speak slowly, and please stop me any time if something is unclear.
  2. Today we are not asking if your work is important. We are asking: if your process stops, how fast does the company have a serious problem? This meeting is recorded, so we have a backup of the information.
  3. I understand — every process matters in daily work. Let’s think about a different question: what happens after eight hours of stop?
  4. A workaround is another way to do the same work when the system is not available. For example, a spreadsheet instead of the system. Do you have one?
  5. Let’s think about the worst moment — for example the end of the month. If the process stops for eight hours, is there a serious impact? What about one day?
  6. Is this vendor exclusive? In other words, can you replace it with another company?

Part 2 · Risk Detective

Case A · Athens form
  • Site: Not critical (smart working)
  • Billing platform: Critical; Email/video: Not critical
  • Maria: Critical (backup untrained)
  • Platform provider: Exclusive + critical
  • Shared folder: Critical
  • Impact: Operative 24–48h · Competitive >48h · Compliance 8–24h · Reputational 24–48h → time limit 8–24 h, priority HIGH
Case B · Lyon form
  • Site: Not critical
  • Customer-data feed: Critical; Email/phones: Not critical
  • Camille’s team: Not critical (two trained backups)
  • Data-centre vendor: Exclusive + critical
  • Laptops and phones: Not critical
  • Impact: Operative 8–24h · Competitive up to 8h · Compliance >48h · Reputational 8–24h → time limit up to 8 h, priority VERY HIGH
Exercise 1 · Memory

site / office, shared drive, cyber attack, earthquake, pandemic, single point of failure, fallback plan, dependency

Exercise 2 · Correct sentence
  1. The process can be blocked for one day. — Modal + be + past participle.
  2. The system was unavailable for many hours. — A period of time takes for; “times” counts repetitions.
  3. This process doesn’t have a workaround. — The process = it → doesn’t.
  4. There is no workaround. — “Workaround” is singular → There is no.
  5. I need to know who the backup is. — Need to + verb.
  6. If the vendor stops, the process will stop. — If + present simple, will + verb.
  7. The people who work here need a backup. — People → who; plural subject → need.
  8. Customers are unable to sign the contract. — “Are unable to” or “cannot” + verb. Never “don’t can”.
Exercise 3 · Formula
  1. The data can be lost.
  2. The system was down for ten hours.
  3. This vendor doesn’t have a competitor.
  4. there is no other way to work.
  5. I need to understand the impact.
  6. If the platform stops, the delay will grow.
  7. People who work on this process need a backup.
  8. The report depends on one analyst.
Exercise 4 · Look-alikes
  • indisponibile → unavailable (not “indisposable”)
  • compilare → fill in / complete (not “compile”)
  • sede → site / office / headquarters (not “seat”)
  • obbligatorio → mandatory / compulsory (“obligatory” is rare)
  • fabbrica → factory (“fabric” = cloth)
  • carburante → fuel (not “carburant”)
  • centrale elettrica → power plant (not “electrical central”)
  • danno → damage (not “danno impact”)
  • eventuale → possible (“eventual” = final)
  • attualmente → currently (“actually” = in fact)
Exercise 5 · Fix the notes
  1. “The billing platform has been unavailable since 10 a.m.” — “Unavailable” + present perfect with since.
  2. “Maria is the only person who knows how to run the final upload.” — person → who; she → knows; “know how to”.
  3. “Her backup hasn’t been trained yet.” — Present perfect passive: hasn’t been trained yet.
  4. “There is no way to create invoices manually.” — There is no way to + verb.
  5. “If the platform stays down for more than one day, the company may receive a fine.” — If + stays (present, -s), may + verb; “receive a fine”.
  6. “We need to know how long the platform can be blocked.” — Duration → how long.
Exercise 6 · Everyday conversations
  1. “Could you please confirm when the service will be restored?”
  2. “I need to let you know that the platform has been unavailable since 10 a.m. We don’t have a workaround yet.”
  3. “If the vendor stops, we will lose our customer data feed for at least three days.”
  4. “How long do you expect the outage to last?”
  5. “We need to train a second person, so that the process doesn’t depend on one individual.”
  6. “The report is due on Friday at 9 a.m., so we have a deadline risk.”
Exercise 7 · Dialogue

Annadora: Thank you for your time. I want to explain the risk in the Lyon process.
Director: Please go ahead. Is the situation serious?
Annadora: Yes. The website receives customer data from one vendor, and the vendor cannot be replaced easily.
Director: How long has the service been unavailable?
Annadora: It has been unavailable for two days.
Director: And what will happen if it stays down?
Annadora: If the vendor does not restore the service this week, the sales team will lose customers.
Director: Is there a workaround?
Annadora: No. There is no other way to receive the data.
Director: Does the team have a backup?
Annadora: Yes, Camille has two colleagues who can do her work.
Director: What do you recommend?
Annadora: We need to sign a second vendor, because today this dependency is a single point of failure.

Exercise 8 · Risk statement

Model answer: If the only vendor in Lyon stops, the sales team will lose its customer data feed. The process can be blocked for up to three days, and there is no workaround. This is critical because customers who cannot sign a contract will choose a competitor. The team has two trained backups, so people are not the problem. However, the vendor is exclusive, so there is no other company that can replace it quickly. We need to sign a second vendor and test a fallback plan, so that the process does not depend on one company.

Exercise 11 · Listen and choose
  1. The vendor doesn’t provide a backup. — Singular vendor → doesn’t; plural → don’t.
  2. They work on the final report. — They → work (no -s). She → works.
  3. Does the process have a workaround? — Singular process → Does; plural → Do.
  4. The systems were unavailable yesterday. — Plural → were.
  5. The person who knows the upload is Maria. — Singular: person who knows is. Plural: people who know are.
  6. The reports need a second check. — Plural reports → need; singular report → needs.
  7. Does he have a backup? — he → Does; you → Do.
  8. We don’t know the procedure. — We → don’t; he → doesn’t.
Exercise 12 · Error hunt

The finance unit prepares the invoices every day. The people who work on this process have a backup, but the backup doesn’t have all the skills. If the platform is blocked for a day, the team can’t create the invoices. Last week the platform was unavailable for two hours, and the vendor restored the service quickly. Does the process have a workaround? No, it doesn’t.

Draft forms (9 wrong, 1 already correct): 1: prepare → prepares, 2: works → work, 3: has → have, 4: don’t have → doesn’t have, 5: will be → is, 6: can’t to → can’t, 7: were → was, 8: restore → restored, 9: Do → Does, 10: doesn’t → doesn’t
